did_you_know.text: The chapter opens with a personal request to the LORD: “Judge me.” David asks the LORD to examine his way of life, and in the same verse he presents three foundations: walking in integrity, trusting in the LORD, and avoiding wrongdoing.

This verse uses several expressions for examination: “Test me,” “try me,” and “refine me.” The psalmist asks that the examination reach his “innermost being and heart”—an expression referring to his inner world, thoughts, and motives.

The psalmist describes the LORD’s steadfast love as something continually before his eyes, and connects remembering that love with walking in truth. Thus, the verse presents a link between reflecting on the LORD’s kindness and living uprightly.

Verses 4–5 describe social and moral separation: the psalmist does not sit with worthless people, associate with hypocrites, or sit with evildoers and the wicked. The repetition of this idea of separation emphasizes the choice of companions and their influence.

“I wash my hands in innocence” begins the transition from turning away from wickedness to drawing near to the worship of the LORD. Clean hands present a picture of purity and proper conduct before the psalmist circles the LORD’s altar.

The purpose of drawing near to the altar is “to proclaim thanksgiving aloud” and to tell of the LORD’s wonders. The verse emphasizes that biblical thanksgiving includes not only an inner feeling, but also speaking and recounting those wonders publicly.

The psalmist declares his love for “the dwelling place of Your house” and “the place where Your glory resides.” Both expressions describe the place of the LORD’s presence and glory, reinforcing the central role of the temple in the prayer of this chapter.

In the final section of the chapter, the psalmist asks not to be gathered together with sinners and men of bloodshed. In the next verse, they are characterized by acts of wickedness and bribery, so the request for deliverance is also a request not to share their moral fate.

After describing the wicked, the psalmist again declares, “But I will walk in my integrity.” Yet he does not rely solely on a claim of innocence; he also asks, “Redeem me and be gracious to me”—seeking redemption and grace from the LORD.

The conclusion presents stability and direction: “My feet stand on level ground.” The psalmist then pledges to bless the LORD among the “assemblies,” meaning before a gathered crowd, so the chapter ends with public testimony rather than private faith alone.
